wine.name: Montes Alpha M
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, about four fifths, with Cabernet Franc and smaller shares of Merlot and Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: The house's Finca de Apalta, on the granite hillsides of the Apalta horseshoe near Santa Cruz; by the house's sheets the fruit comes from the estate's steepest slopes, cropped at low yields.
wine.making: Picked into small boxes in the cool of the day and sorted by bunch and by berry, the fruit falls uncrushed by gravity into stainless steel, soaks cold for about five days and ferments for about ten. The wine then spends eighteen months in French oak barriques, all of them new in the early vintages and most of them in later ones.
wine.glass: Ripe cherry, plum and cassis with a faint note of mint, over cedar, vanilla, tobacco and toast from the oak; concentrated, with dense, silky tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Ready a few years after release, it goes on developing in the cellar for ten years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The house's Bordeaux blend from its Apalta estate, made from the 1996 vintage onwards.
The horseshoe of granite hills near Santa Cruz, an area of the Colchagua Valley under Chile's origin decree since 2018.
The southern zone of the Rapel Valley in Chile's origin decree, warm and inland.

records.table: On granite hillsides at Apalta, near Santa Cruz, Viña Montes grows the Cabernet Sauvignon that leads Montes Alpha M, its Bordeaux blend, given eighteen months in French barriques. The oak shows in cedar and toast over ripe cherry and cassis, the whole concentrated and long.
records.story: The house's own timeline starts with a harvest: in 1987 its founding winemaker and a partner picked the grapes of the first Montes Alpha Cabernet Sauvignon, and in 1988 four partners founded the company under the name Discover Wines; it later took the name Viña Montes, after the winemaker. The partners looked for hillside ground in Colchagua, and the timeline records the purchase of their Apalta estate in 1995: a horseshoe of granite slopes near Santa Cruz, where the vines were cropped low. Alpha M followed with the 1996 vintage, a Bordeaux blend led by Cabernet Sauvignon from the estate's steepest slopes and aged in new French barriques, the first of the flagship wines in the house's timeline. The same hill went on to give the house's Syrah, Montes Folly, from 2000, and part of its Carmenère, Purple Angel, from 2003. In December 2004 Montes opened a new winery on the estate, its design based, the house says, on the principles of feng shui, and the fruit falls by gravity from sorting table to tank. Apalta became an area of Chile's origin decree in 2018. Alpha M marks the moment a Chilean house set out to make a Cabernet blend for the cellar from one hillside.

wine.name: Clos Apalta
wine.grapes: Carmenère, from about half to two thirds, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, and in some years a little Cabernet Franc or Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: Old vines on the estate's Apalta hillside, planted in the early twentieth century from a French massal selection and never grafted, on colluvial granite soils with layers of clay.
wine.making: In the later sheets read, every grape is destemmed by hand at the estate's gravity winery; the 2003 was destemmed by hand only in part. Most of the wine ferments in French oak vats of 75 hectolitres, punched down by hand over four to five weeks on the skins, and goes through malolactic in new barrels. It then ages about two years in French barriques, most of them new, and is bottled without filtration.
wine.glass: Blackberry, blueberry and cassis with clove, black pepper and dried fig, then graphite, cedar, cocoa, leather and tobacco; full and velvety, with fine, polished tannin and a long, smoky finish.
wine.ageing: Made for a long life, by the house's sheets: decant a young bottle or give it several years in the cellar, after which it keeps developing for many more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, 17 by the house's sheets, in a Bordeaux glass; a young bottle wants at least an hour in a decanter.

records.table: Carmenère leads Clos Apalta, Lapostolle's blend from old, ungrafted vines on the Apalta hill, destemmed by hand and aged about two years in French oak, most of it new. In the glass come blackberry, dried fig and tobacco on a velvety texture.
records.story: The family behind Lapostolle made its name in liqueur: an ancestor, Louis-Alexandre Marnier Lapostolle (1857 to 1930), created Grand Marnier, cognac with bitter orange, in 1880. More than a century later his descendants looked to Chile, and in 1994 a couple of the family founded Lapostolle in the Colchagua Valley, with an old vineyard on the Apalta hill at its heart. Its vines had been planted early in the twentieth century from a French massal selection and never grafted. The first Clos Apalta followed with the 1997 vintage, a blend of Merlot, Carmenère and Cabernet Sauvignon. Carmenère, which Chile had long grown as Merlot until the two were told apart in 1994, came to lead the blend. A winery on the slope moves the wine by gravity, and in its later vintages every grape is destemmed by hand before it ferments in large oak vats. The estate's vineyards are farmed organically and biodynamically. When Chile's flagships are listed, Clos Apalta is the wine most often set beside Almaviva, and the reference for Carmenère made to age.

wine.name: Casa Silva Microterroir de Los Lingues Carmenère
wine.grapes: Carmenère alone, from plants selected in each block of the Los Lingues vineyard.
wine.sites: The Los Lingues vineyard on the eastern edge of the Colchagua Valley, in the Andean foothills near San Fernando: clay loam of alluvial and colluvial origin, low in organic matter and fertility, from fine sand to angular granite stones.
wine.making: By the house's sheet for 2021, the berries were sorted a second time and soaked cold for ten days, then fermented in French oak, in barrels of 500 litres and foudres of 1,000 litres, with a long maceration after. Malolactic followed in barrel, and the wine aged fifteen months in French oak.
wine.glass: Ripe red plum and blackberry with a hint of coffee and a soft touch of black pepper; deep ruby with a violet rim, supple, with good structure and soft tannin.
wine.ageing: Drinks well a few years after the vintage and, by the house's account, keeps for about fifteen years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; an hour's decanting suits a young bottle; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The house's name for the vines its soil study picked out, block by block, at Los Lingues.
Part of the wine's name, for the Andean foothill vineyard; an area by the decree of 2018, though the sheet's origin is Colchagua Valley.
The Bordeaux grape Chile long grew as Merlot, bottled here on its own.

records.table: A soil study begun in 2005 with the University of Talca singled out, in each block, the vines of Casa Silva's Microterroir de Los Lingues: Carmenère alone, from the Andean foothills. The grape comes fully ripe here, with red plum, blackberry and a hint of coffee.
records.story: The Silva family's vines in Colchagua go back to a French ancestor from near Saint-Émilion, who reached Chile in the late nineteenth century and, in the family's own history, bought the Angostura estate near San Fernando early in the twentieth. For decades his descendants grew grapes and sold their fruit and wine in bulk to larger houses. In the late 1970s the family began restoring the old vineyards and cellar, and in April 1997, on the proposal of the eldest son of the fifth generation, the family founded Viña Casa Silva to bottle the estate's wine under its own name. The house's vineyard at Los Lingues lies on the eastern edge of the valley at the foot of the Andes, and in 2005 the house began a study of its soils and vines with the University of Talca, which the house describes as the first microterroir study in Chile. Plot by plot, the work showed which ground gave which fruit and guided the replanting, and the Microterroir Carmenère gathers the vines it picked out in each block. In 2018 Chile's origin decree named Los Lingues an area of the valley. The wine's Carmenère comes from a cooler foothill site, picked ripe without the green edge, by a family that measured its ground before it named it.

wine.name: Viu 1
wine.grapes: Malbec, the great majority, with a little Cabernet Sauvignon and in some years a touch of Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: Block 4 of the house's San Carlos vineyard near Cunaco, an old planting of Malbec on alluvial, sandy clay soil with good drainage; the house dates the vines to more than a century ago.
wine.making: After a cold soak of about six days, the must ferments in small stainless steel tanks with short pump overs, about three weeks on the skins in all. Its fifteen months or so in French oak are spent, in recent editions, partly in large untoasted foudres and partly in barriques.
wine.glass: Violet and fresh plum with blueberry and blackberry and a hint of graphite; balanced and concentrated, with fine, velvety tannin and a clear finish that persists.
wine.ageing: It can be drunk on release, after its time in oak, and the house's own pages give it about a decade to develop.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant before serving, as the house advises; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The house's flagship Malbec from Block 4, released in numbered editions from the 1999 vintage.
The origin printed on the label, home to the San Carlos vineyard: the Rapel Valley's southern zone.

records.table: Viu Manent's Viu 1 is old Malbec from Block 4 of the San Carlos vineyard near Cunaco, on sandy clay, scented with violet and plum and fine in tannin. By its own account, the house was first in Chile to bottle Malbec alone under the grape's name, in 1993.
records.story: In 1935 a Catalan immigrant and his two sons founded Bodegas Viu in Santiago, bottling wine for Chilean tables under the Vinos Viu brand. The family wanted vineyards of its own, and in 1966 one of the sons bought the Hacienda San Carlos de Cunaco in the Colchagua Valley, an estate whose old vines, the house says, came from France before phylloxera. Among them were plots of Malbec. In 1993, by the house's own account, Viu Manent became the first Chilean winery to bottle, label and sell a wine of Malbec alone under the grape's name. The house then set its old Malbec block, Block 4 of the San Carlos vineyard, apart, and Viu 1 was first made from the 1999 vintage, as a tribute to the son who had bought the estate. Each vintage made is counted as an edition, the 2021 being the twentieth on the house's sheet, and the bottles are numbered. A little Cabernet Sauvignon joins the Malbec, and recent editions age partly in large, untoasted foudres. Viu 1 answers a guest who thinks of Malbec as Argentina's alone: an old Colchagua block of Malbec, bottled under the grape's name.

wine.name: Neyen Espíritu de Apalta
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon and Carmenère, in near equal parts in the vintages read; early vintages leaned towards Carmenère and some carried Petit Verdot as well.
wine.sites: Old ungrafted vines on the Apalta estate, Cabernet Sauvignon planted around 1890 and Carmenère in 1936 by the house's account, on granite soils washed down from the hills and clay and silt laid by the river.
wine.making: Hand picking early in the morning and two sortings come first; the grapes then ferment with native yeasts in tanks of 5,000 litres over three to four weeks. On the sheets read, each wine spent about fourteen months in French barriques before blending and some six months more in a large foudre.
wine.glass: Raspberry and blackcurrant with cedar, vanilla, leather and a subtle pepper; fresh and composed rather than heavy, with smooth tannin and a finish that lingers.
wine.ageing: It opens a few years after the vintage; merchants' notes give a strong year ten years and more in the cellar.
wine.serve: In a Bordeaux glass at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, after an hour in a decanter if the bottle is young.

label.means: The spirit of Apalta: the meaning of Neyen, the name the house says locals gave the hill's energy.
The valley named as the origin, a zone of the Rapel Valley that takes in the Apalta hill.

records.table: Neyen Espíritu de Apalta joins Cabernet Sauvignon and Carmenère in near equal parts from ungrafted Apalta vines planted around 1890 and in 1936. Fresh rather than heavy, it shows raspberry and blackcurrant with cedar and a subtle pepper.
records.story: Around 1890, by the house's account, Cabernet Sauvignon was planted on the estate's corner of Apalta and the walls of its old winery went up, the oldest in Apalta as the house tells it. Carmenère followed in 1936, and the vines were never grafted. In the early 1970s the Rojas family bought the property and, for decades, sold most of its fruit to others. In 2002 the family created Neyen, which the house glosses as the spirit of Apalta, the energy locals feel on the hill, to bottle a small share of the old vines' fruit under its own name, and the first vintage was the 2003. The blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Carmenère from the old vines has been Neyen's flagship ever since, its shares moving from vintage to vintage. In 2016 the Spanish sherry house González Byass bought a majority of Veramonte, the Chilean company that had taken in Neyen, and with it the Apalta estate. In one glass, then, Neyen pours what old ungrafted vines can give: Cabernet Sauvignon of about 1890 and Carmenère of 1936 from one hill.

others.name: Neyen Ancestral de Apalta Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: Cabernet Sauvignon alone, which the house presents as the rebirth of old vines in its historic Apalta vineyard.

traps: Near equal parts of Cabernet Sauvignon and Carmenère make Neyen Espíritu de Apalta; its neighbour Clos Apalta gives Carmenère the lead.
Not every old vine at Neyen is of one age: the house dates its Cabernet Sauvignon to about 1890 and its Carmenère to 1936.

cards.front: Neyen Espíritu de Apalta: which two grapes, and from vines planted in which years?
cards.back: Cabernet Sauvignon of about 1890 and Carmenère of 1936, both ungrafted, by the house's account.

cards.front: What does the name Neyen mean, as the Apalta house tells it?
cards.back: The spirit of Apalta: the name locals gave the energy of the hill.

questions.q: What sets apart the vines behind Neyen Espíritu de Apalta?
opts: Old ungrafted vines, the eldest planted around 1890

questions.exp: Neyen draws on ungrafted Cabernet Sauvignon of about 1890 and Carmenère of 1936 on the Apalta hill, inland near Santa Cruz, not young grafted vines.

questions.q: Which Spanish house bought a majority of Veramonte, and with it the Neyen estate in Apalta, in 2016?
questions.exp: González Byass of Jerez bought the majority in 2016; Torres came to Chile much earlier, at Curicó in 1979.

report: The plan's why says Carmenère and Cabernet were planted in 1890; the house's page gives 1890 for the Cabernet Sauvignon and 1936 for the Carmenère, while Decanter's merger report gives 1890 for both and another Decanter piece 1889; the record follows the house, and the why may want rewording.

founded is empty: the house claims a winery of 1890; the new winery of 2002 (gravity fed) is in Decanter's merger report and one merchant's copy, and the first Neyen of 2003 in Decanter's Colchagua feature alone, so the story says the early 2000s.

The family that bought the estate is not named or dated: Decanter gives 1970 and a merchant 1973, and its head, Raúl Rojas, may be living (for people.json, with the consultant of the first vintage, Patrick Valette, and the seller of 2016, Agustín Huneeus).
Decanter's report of the Huneeus purchase of Neyen, before 2016, is not cited, because its title and address carry a living person's name; its year was not found.
The Mapuche origin of the name Neyen is common in merchant copy but was not confirmed; the record gives only the house's gloss, the spirit of Apalta.
The first vintage of 2003 was about seventy per cent Carmenère by Decanter; recent vintages run about half and half, so grapes says the early vintages leaned towards Carmenère.
Searches spent on this record: 11 of the author's share of 50; 46 were spent on the group in all.

changed: story, table, wine.sites, cards[0].back, questions[0] and traps[1]: the Cabernet Sauvignon of 1890 is now of about 1890, since the house's accounts give both 1889 for the vines with 1890 for the walls and 1890 for both, and Decanter 1889 in one piece; Carmenère of 1936 stands.
story: the oldest winery in the valley is now the oldest in Apalta, as González Byass's page says.

story: a family bought the property is now the Rojas family in the early 1970s (Decanter 1970, Wine Industry Advisor and a tour guide 1973), and the early 2000s are now 2002 for the creation of Neyen (Wine Industry Advisor, Decanter's merger report) with the 2003 as the first vintage (Decanter's Colchagua feature, and the twentieth year of winemaking marked in 2023).
wine.making: later vintages also use concrete eggs is cut; no source read or cited carries it.
wine.ageing: most critics' windows and the importer's ten years and more, cited by no source, are now merchants' notes of ten years and more for a strong year.
wine.grapes: a little Petit Verdot is now Petit Verdot as well, since the 2006 carried about a sixth of it.
sources: González Byass's British page, a second copy of the house's text, gives way to Wine Industry Advisor's notice of twenty years of winemaking.
open: The native yeasts and the tanks of 5,000 litres rest on the author's reading of the Veramonte sheet; the house's own sheet for 2015 seen here confirms the picking at first light and the double sorting, and merchants the fourteen months in barrel and six in foudre.
founded stays empty: the house dates its winery walls to 1890 and the Neyen label to 2002, and neither is plainly a founding.
The Huneeus link before 2016 (a partnership of 2012 by one account) is not told.
